blocks.text: A tilapia lifted out of a stream dies within minutes, while a catfish in a bucket of damp mud survives for hours. Both need oxygen. The difference lies entirely in the surface each one uses to collect it, and what happens to that surface when it dries.

blocks.markdown:
## What every respiratory surface must have

Gaseous exchange always happens by **diffusion**, so a good respiratory surface is one that makes diffusion fast. Four features are essential:

1. **Large surface area** — more area means more molecules crossing per second.
2. **Thin, usually one cell thick** — a short diffusion distance.
3. **Moist** — gases must dissolve before they can cross a membrane.
4. **Well supplied with blood, or close to the transport medium** — this carries gases away and keeps the concentration gradient steep.

A fifth point applies to larger animals: the surface must be **permeable** and, in land animals, protected inside the body so it does not dry out.

blocks.title: Breathing versus respiration
blocks.text: Breathing (ventilation) is the muscular movement of air into and out of the lungs. Respiration is the chemical release of energy from food inside every cell. A plant respires but does not breathe; a person on a ventilator is being breathed for, but respiration is their own cells' work.

blocks.markdown:
### The human respiratory system

Air travels through the **nostrils**, where it is warmed, moistened and filtered by hairs and mucus, then through the **nasal cavity**, **pharynx**, **larynx** and down the **trachea**. The trachea is held open by C-shaped rings of cartilage; without them the tube would collapse when air pressure inside it fell.

The trachea divides into two **bronchi**, one to each lung, which branch repeatedly into finer **bronchioles**. Each bronchiole ends in a cluster of tiny air sacs, the **alveoli**. Picture a bunch of grapes: the stalk is the bronchiole and each grape is an alveolus, wrapped in a net of capillaries.

There are roughly 700 million alveoli in a pair of human lungs. Each has a wall one cell thick, lined with a film of moisture and pressed against capillaries also one cell thick, so oxygen crosses only two cell layers to reach the blood.

blocks.title: The mechanism of breathing in humans
blocks.prompt: Explain how air is drawn into and forced out of the lungs, and why the lungs themselves play no active part.

steps.text: Inspiration begins with muscle contraction. The external intercostal muscles contract, pulling the ribs upwards and outwards, while the diaphragm muscle contracts and flattens from its domed shape.
The volume of the thoracic cavity therefore increases in all directions.

By the gas laws, increasing the volume lowers the pressure inside the thorax below atmospheric pressure. Air rushes in through the nostrils and trachea until the pressures equalise, and the elastic lungs inflate.
Expiration is largely passive. The external intercostal muscles and diaphragm relax, so the ribs fall under their own weight and the diaphragm returns to its dome shape.

The thoracic volume decreases, the pressure inside rises above atmospheric, and air is forced out. The elastic recoil of the stretched lung tissue assists. In forced expiration the internal intercostal muscles and abdominal muscles contract to push harder.

Note the key point: lung tissue contains no muscle. The lungs are inflated and deflated by pressure changes created by the diaphragm and intercostal muscles, exactly as a balloon inside a syringe would be.

blocks.answer: Inspiration: intercostal muscles and diaphragm contract, thoracic volume increases, pressure falls, air flows in. Expiration: these muscles relax, volume decreases, pressure rises, air flows out. The lungs are passive because they contain no muscle of their own.

blocks.caption: Composition of inspired and expired air. Nitrogen is unchanged because the body does not use it.

blocks.title: Surface area to volume ratio
blocks.text: As an organism gets bigger, its volume grows faster than its surface area. A single-celled Amoeba can get all its oxygen through its surface, but a goat of the same shape scaled up could not — which is why large animals evolved specialised, highly folded respiratory organs such as gills and lungs.

blocks.title: Explain, do not just name
blocks.text: If asked why an earthworm dies in dry soil, do not write 'because its skin is dry'. Write that gases must dissolve in moisture before they can diffuse across the surface, so a dry skin cannot absorb oxygen and the worm suffocates.

points: A respiratory surface must be large, thin, moist and well supplied with blood or close to the transport medium.
Amoeba uses its cell surface, the earthworm its moist skin, fish their gills, insects a tracheal system, and mammals lungs with alveoli.
Breathing is the muscular ventilation of the lungs; respiration is the release of energy inside cells.
Inspiration results from contraction of the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles, which raises thoracic volume and lowers pressure.
Expired air contains less oxygen and about a hundred times more carbon dioxide than inspired air, but the same amount of nitrogen.
